prompt: Merge k sorted lists with N total elements. There are 1,000 lists and one million elements. Which approach explicitly keeps only the current nonempty list heads in a heap, with the stated complexity? Assume constant-cost comparisons and amortised heap operations.

options.text: A min-heap of current heads: O(k + N log(k + 1))
options.explanation: Correct. Keep one head per nonempty list, then pop and replenish one head per output. Inspecting k inputs and producing N outputs costs O(k + N log(k + 1)); the worked example’s figures are growth expressions, not exact heap comparison counts.

options.text: Concatenate and sort: O(N log N)
options.explanation: This does not use the requested heap-of-heads method. A generic sort has an O(N log N) bound, but adaptive sorting, including Python’s sort, can exploit existing runs and need not do twice the heap’s work. Concatenating materialises N items.

options.text: Merge the lists into a running result one at a time: O(N·k)
options.explanation: Each merge re-copies the growing result: with equal-sized lists and sequential growing-result merges, that is roughly half of N times k, about 5 × 10⁸ output-element writes; uneven sizes change this count.

options.text: Scan all k heads to find the smallest each time: O(N log k)
options.explanation: A linear scan of k heads costs O(k) per output element, so this is O(N·k), about 10⁹ operations here.

workedExample:
Compare how each approach's work grows. A heap of 1,000 heads is about 10 levels deep, so a million outputs give a growth figure of about 10 million; a generic sort of a million items involves about 20 halvings, about 20 million. Merging into a growing result recopies it repeatedly (about 500 million writes for equal-sized lists), and scanning all 1,000 heads for each output is about a billion steps. These are growth figures, not measured times.

| Approach | Generic cost expression | Illustrative expression value |
|---|---|---|
| Sort all | O(N log N) | ~2 × 10⁷ |
| Sequential merge | O(Nk) | ~5 × 10⁸ |
| Heap of heads | O(k + N log(k + 1)) | ~10⁷ |
| Scan heads | O(Nk) | ~10⁹ |

The heap only ever holds k items, one per list. That's why external sorts and LSM-tree compactions use it: they can stream through files far bigger than memory.
